questions.scenario: A physician owns only four stocks, all in health care. He says, 'I understand this industry better than any outsider,' and refuses to consider an index fund or any other sector.
questions.explanation: He overrates what he knows and takes concentrated risk because of it. That is overconfidence. Affinity bias would be choosing investments to express identity or loyalty, rather than from belief in an informational edge.

questions.scenario: After completing an online course on options, a novice sells uncovered puts on margin. He says the course gave him 'an institutional-level edge' and that he understands the risk, though he cannot explain what would happen in a sharp selloff.
questions.explanation: A little knowledge leaves him far more certain than is justified, and he takes dangerous risks as a result. That is overconfidence. Illusion of control would be believing he can influence the outcome itself.

questions.scenario: A portfolio manager says that there is a 'near-zero' chance a favored stock will fall below $60. It falls to $41, and he calls himself 'just early.' His next forecast has an equally narrow range.
questions.explanation: He gives ranges that are too narrow and does not widen them after being wrong. That is overconfidence. Conservatism would mean under-updating after new information.

questions.scenario: A recent retiree withdraws 9% of his portfolio a year to pay for cruises and gifts to his grandchildren, even though he knows his plan sustainably supports about 4%. He says he 'deserves to enjoy it now' and will 'deal with it later.'
questions.explanation: Present gratification wins over his long-term goal of lasting financial security, despite his knowing the plan's limits. Failing to act on long-term goals because of insufficient discipline in the moment is self-control bias.

questions.scenario: Employees in a workplace survey say that they know they should save more for retirement but 'can't bring themselves to cut spending today.' Many say they would be willing to commit to higher contributions only out of future pay raises.
questions.explanation: They recognize the long-term benefit of saving but cannot give up current consumption. The conflict between present gratification and future benefit is self-control bias, which is why pre-commitment designs such as Thaler and Benartzi's 'Save More Tomorrow' work better than willpower.

questions.scenario: A 40-year-old with a 25-year horizon holds 70% of his portfolio in high-yield, income-producing products, saying, 'I like having the cash flow to spend now.' His advisor points out that he needs more growth assets to outpace inflation before retirement.
questions.explanation: A 'spend-today' mentality skews his portfolio toward income at the expense of the long-term growth he needs. A portfolio heavily tilted to income because of a desire for current spending may reflect self-control bias rather than a real income need.

questions.scenario: An investor keeps promising himself he will set up an automatic monthly investment, but every month the money goes on small purchases and dining out. After ten years of 'I'll start next month,' he has missed a decade of compounding.
questions.explanation: He fails to act on his long-term goal because spending now is more gratifying, and so misses compounding and dollar-cost averaging. The remedy is 'paying yourself first' with automated, pre-committed savings, a classic response to self-control bias.

questions.scenario: In a retirement survey, households that never sat down to plan for retirement had saved markedly less than those who did, held fewer stocks, and were far more likely to rate their expected retirement quality of life as poor.
questions.explanation: Failing to plan and save for the future despite knowing it matters is the hallmark of self-control bias. Annamaria Lusardi's research found that non-planners save much less, own fewer stocks and rate their retirement outlook worse.

questions.scenario: A man who tends to overspend on weekends has part of every paycheck moved into a locked retirement account, saying, 'I don't trust myself with cash.'
questions.explanation: He knows that his urge to spend now will beat his long-term goals, so he uses a commitment device. That is a self-control problem. Mental accounting would be about treating money differently by bucket, not about managing impulses.

questions.scenario: A trader's plan is to invest for the long run, but he keeps day trading because of the thrill of quick wins. He admits to friends that it is costing him money.
questions.explanation: He knows what he should do, but present gratification wins over the long-term goal. That is a lack of self-control. Illusion of control would be thinking his trading skill beats chance, which he does not claim.

questions.scenario: A healthy 62-year-old claims Social Security at the earliest age to fund travel now, although waiting would raise his benefit by about 8% a year and he has no pressing need for the money.
questions.explanation: He prefers immediate spending to a clearly larger later benefit. That is a self-control problem.

questions.scenario: A lottery winner plans to save half of his $2 million prize, but each month he finds a reason to spend instead. Within three years the money is gone.
questions.explanation: He has a long-term plan, but present gratification keeps winning. That is a self-control problem. Mental accounting would apply if he treated the windfall differently from other money, but the cue is the failure to follow his own plan.

questions.scenario: A graduate with $12,000 of credit card debt at 21% signs up for a store card to get 15% off a TV he cannot afford. He says he meant to cut his spending, but 'it's just so tempting.'
questions.explanation: He has the goal of cutting spending but cannot resist the immediate pleasure. That is a self-control problem. Framing would involve reacting to the presentation of the discount rather than to the temptation.

questions.scenario: Two neighboring states reform their auto-insurance rules. In the state where drivers are defaulted into the more expensive plan with full litigation rights, about 70% keep it. In the other state, where drivers are defaulted into a cheaper plan with limited rights, about 80% keep that one.
questions.explanation: What people ended up with tracked the default rather than any stable underlying preference, because people tend to prefer whatever maintains the current state of affairs. This New Jersey/Pennsylvania example is the classic illustration of status quo bias.

questions.scenario: When an employee joined his company 12 years ago, his 401(k) was automatically invested in a money-market fund. His statements show he is earning less than inflation, and he admits a diversified target-date fund would be better. He has never changed the allocation, saying, 'It's fine as it is.'
questions.explanation: He sticks with the default option regardless of whether an alternative would objectively be better. Preferring to leave things as they are is status quo bias, and it persists even though he knows the facts.

questions.scenario: A client has paid the same advisory fee and held the same set of funds for fifteen years, though cheaper equivalent options now exist. When asked, he says he never compared them because switching is 'not worth thinking about' and his current arrangement is 'good enough.'
questions.explanation: He keeps the current arrangement simply because it is the current arrangement, without any real evaluation of alternatives. A preference for maintaining the existing state of affairs, independent of whether a change would be better, is status quo bias.

questions.scenario: A company changes its retirement plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment with an opt-out option. Participation jumps from about 40% to about 90%, although the plan's terms, contribution rates and investment choices are unchanged.
questions.explanation: Most people stay with whatever option is set as the default, so changing the default changes the outcome. That tendency to stick with the current state of affairs is status quo bias.

questions.scenario: A widow has kept her late husband's portfolio exactly as he built it for fifteen years and has never rebalanced. The allocation is now too aggressive for her low risk tolerance and her need for income, but she says, 'I'd rather not touch it.' She has no strong attachment to any particular holding.
questions.explanation: She leaves the portfolio as it is even though it no longer fits her needs, and not because she values any particular holding. A preference for keeping things unchanged, regardless of whether a change would be better, is status quo bias.

questions.scenario: Customers who have been with an auto insurer for six years pay about 20% more than new customers for the same coverage. Fewer than one in five of them ever shops around.
questions.explanation: They stay with the current policy by default even though switching would save money. That is status quo bias. Endowment bias would be valuing the policy more because they own it.

questions.scenario: In an experiment, subjects choose among investment options. When one option is described as their current holding, a much larger share choose it than when the same option is presented as one of several new choices.
questions.explanation: The current holding is chosen mainly because it is the current state of affairs. That is status quo bias, as in Samuelson and Zeckhauser's studies. Endowment bias would be valuing it more because it is theirs.

questions.scenario: In one country, citizens are organ donors unless they opt out, and about 90% are donors. In a neighboring country, citizens must opt in, and about 15% are donors.
questions.explanation: People mostly stick with whichever default they are given. That is status quo bias. Framing would involve different descriptions of the same options rather than a different default.

questions.scenario: A review of 1.2 million retirement-plan participants finds that about 80% made no change to their allocation over ten years, even though their ages and market conditions changed greatly.
questions.explanation: Participants leave their allocation as it is regardless of changing circumstances. That is status quo bias. Self-control problems could explain a failure to save, but here the pattern is inertia.

questions.scenario: Each year a city council sets its budget at last year's level plus 2%, even for a program whose use has dropped by half over the last decade, because 'that's how the budget has always been done.'
questions.explanation: The current arrangement continues simply because it is the current one. That is status quo bias. Anchoring would be fixation on a number given for a specific estimate.

questions.scenario: A client owns a stock that he would pay at most $38 for if he were buying it today, yet he refuses to sell it for less than $52. He cannot point to any news or fundamentals that would explain the gap.
questions.explanation: The price he demands to give up the stock is far above the price he would pay to acquire it, simply because he owns it. That gap between willingness to accept and willingness to pay is the endowment effect.

questions.scenario: In an experiment, half the participants are given a coffee mug and half are given a candy bar. Before being given anything, the group split roughly 50/50 on which item they preferred. Afterward, about 90% of each group refuse to swap what they were given for the other item.
questions.explanation: Merely being given an item makes people value it more than the alternative. This is Knetsch's mug-and-candy experiment, the standard demonstration of endowment bias.

questions.scenario: A man inherits his father's shares in a regional brewery. He would never have picked the stock himself and would not buy it today, but he refuses to sell and values the shares well above their market price, because they are now 'his' shares.
questions.explanation: He values the shares more highly than he otherwise would simply because he owns them. Inherited securities are a common form of endowment bias, and a good test is to ask what he would do if he had received the same value in cash.

questions.scenario: At a sports-card show, novice collectors refuse to trade a card they own for another card of equal market value. Professional dealers at the same show trade freely, showing little reluctance to part with what they own.
questions.explanation: Novices demand more to give up cards they own than the cards are worth to them as buyers, while experienced traders do not. John List's finding that the effect shrinks with trading experience is a hallmark of the endowment effect.

questions.scenario: A homeowner is convinced his house is worth $450,000 and rejects offers up to $420,000, even though comparable houses nearby sell for about $415,000. He says he would not pay more than $415,000 for an identical house if it belonged to someone else.
questions.explanation: He values what he owns more highly than he would value the same thing as a buyer. A gap between what you would pay and what you would demand to give up the same asset is the endowment effect.

questions.scenario: Office workers are randomly handed lottery tickets. Those given tickets demand much more to sell them than other workers are willing to pay for the same ticket.
questions.explanation: Ownership, even if random, raises the value people place on a ticket. That is endowment bias. Illusion of control would apply only if workers chose their own numbers.

questions.scenario: A woman is given 100 shares of her employer's stock as a gift and refuses to diversify, saying, 'It's my company's stock and I know what I have.' She admits that she would not buy it with her own money at today's price.
questions.explanation: She values the shares more because they are hers, which is endowment bias. Affinity bias would involve choosing a stock because of loyalty or identity, rather than being reluctant to part with one she owns.

questions.scenario: A comic-book collector inherits a set. He turns down an offer of $2,000 saying that it is 'worth much more,' even though he passed on an identical set priced at $1,200 at a shop last month.
questions.explanation: He demands more to give up the set he owns than he would pay to get the same one. That is endowment bias.

questions.scenario: A software firm offers a 60-day free trial of its premium plan. Users must enter card details to continue in both cases, yet 70% of those who had the trial subscribe, against 20% of a control group offered the plan with no trial.
questions.explanation: After using the product, people value it more because it feels like theirs. That is endowment bias. Status quo bias would require that subscribing be the default, which it is not.

questions.scenario: A survey finds that founders typically value their start-ups at two to three times what investors are willing to pay, even when the founders have seen comparable deals.
questions.explanation: Owners value what they own more than outsiders do. That is endowment bias. Overconfidence could contribute, but the gap between the seller's and the buyer's valuation is the cue.

questions.scenario: After losing money in the 2008 crash, an investor keeps all of his savings in cash for ten years and misses a long recovery. He says that if he bought stocks and watched them fall again, he would 'kick myself for making the decision,' so he prefers not to decide.
questions.explanation: His real fear is the emotional pain of having made a decision that turns out wrong, so he avoids acting and becomes too conservative after a past loss. Avoiding decisive action to avoid regret is regret aversion bias. The cue is the pain of the decision, not just the loss itself.

questions.scenario: Jim must choose between a famous large company and an unknown mid-sized company with the same expected return and risk. He picks the famous one, explaining that if it falls he can say 'everybody lost money on it,' while a loss on the obscure one would make him look foolish.
questions.explanation: The two investments are financially equivalent, but a loss on a well-known name feels less personally foolish. Choosing the option that would cause less regret if it fails is regret aversion bias.

questions.scenario: An investor buys a hot stock only because everyone around him is buying it. He says, 'If it fails, at least I won't be the only one who got burned.' He has not tied the purchase to any financial goal of his own.
questions.explanation: Following the crowd diffuses individual blame if the investment goes wrong. This kind of herding is a way of avoiding the pain of regret, so it is a manifestation of regret aversion.

questions.scenario: A stock an investor owns has doubled and is now showing signs of weakness. He does not sell, because if he sold and the stock kept rising, he would feel awful for having let it go.
questions.explanation: He holds the winner too long out of fear of regretting a sale that is followed by more gains. Loss aversion would predict selling a winner early. The cue is the anticipated regret of an action (selling), which is regret aversion.

questions.scenario: A retiree insists on spending only his stocks' dividends rather than selling shares to raise the same amount of cash. He says selling feels like a decision he might regret if the price later rose, while dividends 'just arrive.'
questions.explanation: Selling shares is an active decision (an error of commission if it goes wrong), while spending dividends feels like inaction, even though the two are financially equivalent. Shefrin and Statman tie this preference for dividends to regret aversion.

questions.scenario: A pension fund keeps its portfolio close to that of its peers, and the chief investment officer says, 'No one gets fired for following the pack.'
questions.explanation: The fund avoids being singled out for a bad decision, even if it gives up a better opportunity. That is regret aversion. Status quo bias would be inertia, not the fear of looking wrong.

questions.scenario: An investor sold a stock that then doubled. He vows never to sell anything again and holds on to every position, even when it falls sharply.
questions.explanation: He avoids decisive action to prevent the pain of regret. That is regret aversion. Loss aversion would be about the pain of losses, not the fear of regretting a decision.

questions.scenario: An investor with $200,000 in cash from a home sale keeps putting off investing, for fear that the market will drop right after he buys. If it falls, he feels vindicated; if it rises, he feels sick.
questions.explanation: He is trying to avoid the regret of buying at the wrong time. That is regret aversion. Self-control problems would be about giving in to temptation, not about worrying over future regret.

questions.scenario: In a classic experiment, George considered switching from stock A to stock B but did not, and lost $1,200. Paul switched from stock B to A and lost $1,200. Most people say that Paul feels worse.
questions.explanation: Regret is stronger for a loss that follows action than for an equal loss that follows inaction, so people are drawn to avoid action. That is regret aversion.

questions.scenario: A saver rejects an annuity from a small insurer with a higher payout and picks a pricier big-name insurer, so that if the insurer fails, nobody can say, 'You should have known.'
questions.explanation: She chooses the option that is easiest to defend afterward. That is regret aversion. Affinity bias would be choosing based on identity or values.

questions.scenario: A woman loves a trendy fashion brand's clothes and puts a large share of her savings into the company's stock. She has not looked at the company's debt, margins or earnings, saying, 'I just love what they stand for.'
questions.explanation: She invests because the company's products reflect her tastes and self-image (expressive value), rather than because she has checked its financial soundness. That is affinity bias.

questions.scenario: An investor buys a fund solely because its name and mission match his values. He does not review its fees, holdings or past performance, saying 'it just feels right.'
questions.explanation: Choosing an investment based on how well it reflects personal values, without equally rigorous financial due diligence, is affinity bias. The caution is about skipping the diligence, not about values-based investing itself.

questions.scenario: A wealthy client demands access to an exclusive hedge fund because his friends at the golf club invest in it. He cannot explain its strategy or its risks, but says being in the fund 'says something about who I am.'
questions.explanation: He values the fund for its status and image and for belonging to a peer group, rather than for its risk and return characteristics. Chasing 'status' investments to signal sophistication is affinity bias.

questions.scenario: During a period of political tension with another country, American investors sell shares of that country's companies traded in the U.S. Demand drops measurably, even though nothing about the companies' fundamentals has changed.
questions.explanation: Investors let loyalty and sentiment, rather than financial merit, drive their holdings. Morse and Shive's research on patriotism in portfolios, which found that U.S. demand for French ADRs dropped during anti-French sentiment, illustrates affinity bias.

questions.scenario: An American investor keeps 92% of his equity in U.S. companies because he wants to 'invest in America' and does not 'trust foreign markets.' A globally diversified mix would hold only about a third in U.S. stocks.
questions.explanation: He overweights domestic securities out of loyalty and a sense of national identity rather than optimal diversification. This patriotism or home-country bias is a well-studied form of affinity bias.

questions.scenario: Members of a church congregation invest heavily in a high-yield scheme run by one of the church elders, without any due diligence, because 'he is one of us.'
questions.explanation: They pick the investment because of shared identity and loyalty instead of financial merit. That is affinity bias. Representativeness would be judging by resemblance to a success story.

questions.scenario: An investor whose family has worked in the auto industry for three generations owns only car-company stock. He admits that the numbers are poor but says, 'We are a car family.'
questions.explanation: He invests to express his identity and loyalty and not for financial merit. That is affinity bias. Endowment bias would be valuing something more simply because it is owned.

questions.scenario: A venture angel invests only in start-ups run by alumni of his university and spends little time on the financial statements. His portfolio lags the market for early-stage investments.
questions.explanation: He chooses by shared background instead of merit. That is affinity bias.

questions.scenario: A baseball fan buys shares of the company that owns his favorite team, saying he wants to 'feel part of it,' though the stock has trailed the market for ten years.
questions.explanation: He buys to express loyalty rather than for financial reasons. That is affinity bias.

questions.scenario: A client picks a financial advisor only because the advisor attends the same church and supports the same political party. The client does not check the advisor's track record or fees.
questions.explanation: Shared identity, rather than competence, drives the choice. That is affinity bias. Confirmation bias would require that he collect evidence to support a prior belief.
